hero.headline: Switch people on.
hero.subheadline: The science behind how great leaders educate, communicate, and facilitate — and how Mentimeter makes it happen.

scienceSkills.headline: Reset Attention Continuously
scienceSkills.problem: Attention fluctuates. People drift — not because they don't care, but because passive listening isn't enough to stay present.
scienceSkills.solution: Build interaction moments into every session to re-orient focus and bring people back into active processing.

back.principle: Attention is limited and decays over time without stimulation. Passive listening leads to shallow processing.
back.whatHappened: You were asked a question — and you started thinking.
back.whyItWorks: Questions don't just ask for answers. They activate attention and create a sense of involvement.
back.scienceBehind: Attention systems require periodic reactivation. Multimedia learning research confirms that interaction points improve retention and engagement.
back.inPractice: Don't let people listen for more than a few minutes without a question or interaction. Use pulse checks, quick polls, or open questions to reset.

scienceSkills.headline: Reduce Cognitive Overload
scienceSkills.problem: Working memory is small. Too much information at once leads to confusion, not comprehension.
scienceSkills.solution: Break content into smaller, focused parts. One idea at a time. One question at a time.

back.principle: Cognitive Load Theory shows that excess information degrades understanding. The brain needs space to process.
back.whatHappened: When content was chunked, you followed it — when it wasn't, you lost the thread.
back.whyItWorks: Structure reduces the cognitive effort needed to follow and understand content.
back.scienceBehind: Working memory can hold roughly 4±1 items at a time. Overloading it blocks learning and reduces decision quality.
back.inPractice: Structure beats density. Remove slides, split long questions, and pause before moving on.

scienceSkills.headline: Protect Individual Thinking
scienceSkills.problem: Early opinions anchor the group. The loudest voice shapes everyone else's view before they've had time to think.
scienceSkills.solution: Capture individual input before any group discussion begins — ideally anonymously.

back.principle: Social influence and information sampling bias show that group discussion often narrows rather than expands thinking.
back.whatHappened: When you answered before seeing others' responses, your answer was genuinely yours.
back.whyItWorks: Anonymity and individual-first sequencing preserve independent judgment.
back.scienceBehind: Conformity research (Asch) and hidden profile studies (Stasser) show groups systematically suppress minority views without structure.
back.inPractice: Always ask people to respond individually before revealing results or opening discussion.

scienceSkills.headline: Make Thinking Visible
scienceSkills.problem: Assumptions and patterns stay hidden in people's heads. What isn't shared can't be challenged or built upon.
scienceSkills.solution: Externalize input so individuals and groups can see, compare, and make sense of what matters.

back.principle: Shared information becomes group knowledge only when it is externalized. Hidden assumptions drive poor decisions.
back.whatHappened: When responses were displayed, you saw patterns and perspectives you didn't know existed.
back.whyItWorks: Visibility creates a shared object to react to, discuss, and decide from.
back.scienceBehind: Self-explanation and externalization research shows that making thinking visible improves individual understanding and collective sense-making.
back.inPractice: Use word clouds, open text, and rating distributions to surface what would otherwise stay inside people's heads.

scienceSkills.headline: Use Retrieval Instead of Repetition
scienceSkills.problem: Repeating information doesn't strengthen memory. People hear the same thing and forget it just the same.
scienceSkills.solution: Ask people to recall information before reviewing it. The act of retrieval is the learning.

back.principle: The 'testing effect' — retrieving information from memory strengthens memory traces more than re-reading or re-listening.
back.whatHappened: When asked 'What do you remember?', you worked harder — and retained more.
back.whyItWorks: Effortful retrieval creates stronger memory consolidation than passive re-exposure.
back.scienceBehind: Test-Enhanced Learning research shows retrieval practice produces more durable learning than elaborative studying.
back.inPractice: Start sessions with 'What do you remember from last week?' before presenting anything new.

scienceSkills.headline: Let People Generate Their Own Answers
scienceSkills.problem: When people receive the answer first, they process it passively — and remember little of it.
scienceSkills.solution: Ask people to generate their own answer before revealing the solution or insight.

back.principle: The 'generation effect' — self-generated material is better retained than passively received material.
back.whatHappened: When asked for your opinion before being told the answer, you thought harder.
back.whyItWorks: Generation creates effortful processing and deeper encoding in long-term memory.
back.scienceBehind: Producing material requires active engagement with prior knowledge, creating stronger memory traces than passive reception.
back.inPractice: Before sharing a key insight, ask people to generate their own answer first. Then reveal and compare.

scienceSkills.headline: Activate Prior Knowledge
scienceSkills.problem: New information floats without an anchor. Without connection to what people already know, it doesn't stick.
scienceSkills.solution: Start every learning moment by asking what people already know or believe about the topic.

back.principle: Prior knowledge activation improves subsequent learning by creating cognitive hooks for new information.
back.whatHappened: Before being taught, you were asked what you already knew — making the new information feel connected.
back.whyItWorks: Learning builds on existing structures. Activating them first makes new content easier to integrate.
back.scienceBehind: Schema theory and constructivist learning research show that prior knowledge is the strongest predictor of new learning.
back.inPractice: Open every training or presentation with a question about existing knowledge or belief on the topic.

scienceSkills.headline: Reinforce Over Time
scienceSkills.problem: One-off sessions don't change performance. Without follow-up, learning fades within days.
scienceSkills.solution: Space out questions and practice moments over time to strengthen long-term memory retention.

back.principle: The 'spacing effect' — distributed practice produces stronger retention than massed practice (cramming).
back.whatHappened: Revisiting content days later — not just once — is what makes it stay.
back.whyItWorks: Each retrieval after a delay re-consolidates the memory, making it more durable.
back.scienceBehind: Forgetting curve research shows memory decays rapidly without reinforcement. Spaced repetition counteracts this.
back.inPractice: Build follow-up questions, check-ins, and micro-practice moments into the days and weeks after any learning event.

scienceSkills.headline: Learn Socially
scienceSkills.problem: Individual reflection has limits. Without discussing and comparing with others, understanding stays shallow.
scienceSkills.solution: After individual thinking, share and compare — use the diversity of responses as the teaching moment.

back.principle: Social learning increases cognitive engagement, motivation, and retention through discussion and comparison.
back.whatHappened: Seeing how others responded to the same question expanded your own thinking.
back.whyItWorks: Explaining and comparing ideas with others forces deeper processing than solo reflection.
back.scienceBehind: Collaborative learning research shows that articulating ideas to others improves understanding and long-term retention.
back.inPractice: Show results after individual responses and use the distribution to guide a short discussion.

scienceSkills.headline: Distribute Participation
scienceSkills.problem: A few voices dominate. Most people stay silent — not because they have nothing to say, but because the structure doesn't invite them.
scienceSkills.solution: Use tools and formats that ensure everyone contributes, not just the confident or the senior.

back.principle: Groups that hear from all members make better decisions. Broad participation improves idea diversity and collective performance.
back.whatHappened: When everyone submitted a response simultaneously, the room's full range of thinking became visible.
back.whyItWorks: Equal participation reduces dominance effects and surfaces knowledge held by quieter people.
back.scienceBehind: Collective intelligence research shows that the strongest predictor of team performance is equal distribution of speaking time.
back.inPractice: Anonymous contribution tools level the playing field. Set the expectation: everyone answers before anyone speaks.

scienceSkills.headline: Surface Disagreement & Diverse Perspectives
scienceSkills.problem: Groups converge too quickly. Agreement can hide weak thinking, unspoken doubt, and unconsidered options.
scienceSkills.solution: Actively surface disagreement and minority views before converging on a decision.

back.principle: Groupthink and cascade effects suppress minority views. Diverse perspectives improve decisions.
back.whatHappened: When the spread of opinions was displayed, you saw the disagreement that would have stayed hidden.
back.whyItWorks: Visible disagreement challenges assumptions and triggers deeper evaluation of options.
back.scienceBehind: Deviant minority research (Nemeth) shows that minority viewpoints — even when wrong — improve group decision quality by prompting deeper analysis.
back.inPractice: Visualize the spread of opinions. If everyone agrees immediately, treat that as a signal to probe further.

scienceSkills.headline: Clarify Decision Type & Criteria
scienceSkills.problem: People evaluate options inconsistently when the decision type and success criteria aren't defined upfront.
scienceSkills.solution: Define what you're deciding and what a good decision looks like before evaluating any options.

back.principle: Noise — inconsistency in judgment — decreases dramatically when criteria are shared and explicit.
back.whatHappened: When the decision and evaluation criteria were set upfront, your input was more focused and useful.
back.whyItWorks: Shared criteria align thinking and reduce the variance in how people evaluate the same options.
back.scienceBehind: Decision science research shows that inconsistent judgments (noise) are as damaging as bias — and harder to detect.
back.inPractice: Before any vote or evaluation: ask 'What are we deciding, and what does a good decision look like here?'

scienceSkills.headline: Goal Clarity & Specificity
scienceSkills.problem: Vague goals produce vague effort. 'Do your best' is not a strategy.
scienceSkills.solution: Set clear, specific goals and success criteria before any session or initiative begins.

back.principle: Goal-setting theory shows that specific, challenging goals drive higher performance than vague or easy ones.
back.whatHappened: When the outcome was defined clearly before the session started, thinking became more directed.
back.whyItWorks: Specificity creates focus. When people know what success looks like, they allocate effort more effectively.
back.scienceBehind: Decades of goal-setting research (Locke & Latham) show that specificity and challenge are the two strongest predictors of goal performance.
back.inPractice: Start every meeting or training with: 'What outcome are we trying to achieve, and how will we know we succeeded?'

scienceSkills.headline: Implementation Intentions
scienceSkills.problem: Good intentions don't automatically become actions. The gap between 'I will' and 'I did' is where most change fails.
scienceSkills.solution: Link intended behaviors to specific situations: 'If X happens, then I will do Y.'

back.principle: If–then planning bridges the intention–action gap by pre-deciding behavior in specific contexts.
back.whatHappened: When asked 'When specifically will you do this?', the commitment became concrete.
back.whyItWorks: Linking an intention to a specific trigger removes the need for in-the-moment decision-making.
back.scienceBehind: Implementation intention research shows 2–3× higher follow-through rates compared to simple goal-setting.
back.inPractice: End sessions with: 'What will you do differently — and when and where specifically will you do it?'

scienceSkills.headline: Create Psychological Safety
scienceSkills.problem: People hold back when there is social risk. The most important ideas stay unspoken.
scienceSkills.solution: Design for safety: use anonymity, model openness, and make it genuinely easy to speak up.

back.principle: Teams with high psychological safety outperform those without — across all measures of performance.
back.whatHappened: When responses were anonymous, people shared what they actually thought.
back.whyItWorks: Removing social risk increases honesty, openness, and cognitive flexibility.
back.scienceBehind: Edmondson's team research shows psychological safety is the single strongest predictor of team learning and performance.
back.inPractice: Anonymity is a design tool, not a fallback. Build it in by default for sensitive or evaluative questions.

scienceSkills.headline: Build Feedback Loops
scienceSkills.problem: Progress stalls without feedback. People don't know if they're improving — or how.
scienceSkills.solution: Provide timely, specific feedback that makes progress visible and actionable.

back.principle: Feedback is one of the most powerful drivers of behavior change — but only when it is timely and actionable.
back.whatHappened: Seeing your results immediately and in context of others gave you something concrete to respond to.
back.whyItWorks: Feedback closes the loop between effort and outcome, enabling learning and course-correction.
back.scienceBehind: Meta-analysis of feedback research (Hattie) shows it has one of the highest effect sizes on learning of any intervention.
back.inPractice: Show results immediately. Let people see how their input compared to others. Make learning visible in the room.
